content: 1. Ciprofloxacin can increase the levels of timolol by reducing its metabolism. This interaction is considered minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. Rarely, ciprofloxacin may also decrease beta-blocker levels. Close monitoring is recommended. 2. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of tinidazole by inhibiting the hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution should be exercised, and close monitoring is advised. 3. Ciprofloxacin significantly increases the levels or effects of tizanidine by inhibiting hepatic enzyme CYP1A2 metabolism. Co-administration of ciprofloxacin and tizanidine is contraindicated. Alternative drugs should be used, and concurrent use should be avoided. 4. Inhaled tobramycin and ciprofloxacin together increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is required. Concurrent or sequential use should be avoided to reduce the risk of ototoxicity. 5. Ciprofloxacin and tolmetin may increase the risk of central nervous system (CNS) stimulation and seizures, particularly at high doses of fluoroquinolones. The mechanism is unknown. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. 6. Ciprofloxacin and toremifene both prolong the QTc interval, increasing the risk of serious cardiac arrhythmias. Concurrent use should be avoided, and alternative drugs should be considered. If concomitant use is necessary, toremifene should be interrupted, or patients should be closely monitored with ECGs, especially those at high risk. 7. Ciprofloxacin and tretinoin (oral or topical) both increase the risk of phototoxicity due to pharmacodynamic synergism. Concomitant use should be avoided, and alternative drugs should be considered. If used together, caution is advised. 8. Ciprofloxacin and injectable triamcinolone acetonide may increase the risk of tendon rupture when quinolone antibiotics and corticosteroids are co-administered. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 9. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels of triazolam by reducing its metabolism. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 10. Trilaciclib decreases the levels or effects of ciprofloxacin by inhibiting OCT2, MATE1, and MATE-2K transporters. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative drugs should be used. Minimal increases in substrate concentrations in the kidney or blood may lead to serious or life-threatening toxicities. 11. Trimagnesium citrate anhydrous reduces ciprofloxacin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Ciprofloxacin should be administered at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after magnesium-containing products. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 12. Ciprofloxacin and triptorelin both prolong the QTc interval, increasing the risk of torsades de pointes. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 13. Tucatinib increases the levels or effects of ciprofloxacin by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Caution and close monitoring are advised. Dosage reduction of P-gp substrates should be considered to avoid serious or life-threatening toxicities. 14. Ciprofloxacin reduces the efficacy of the live typhoid vaccine due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Co-administration is contraindicated. Antibiotics may diminish the therapeutic effects of live bacterial vaccines. Vaccination should be delayed until antibiotic treatment is completed. 15. Ciprofloxacin increases the toxicity of umeclidinium bromide/vilanterol inhaled by prolonging the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative drugs should be used. Extreme caution is required when vilanterol is co-administered with drugs that prolong the QTc interval, as adrenergic agonist effects on the cardiovascular system may be potentiated. 16. Vadadustat increases the levels or effects of ciprofloxacin by affecting OAT3 substrates. Close monitoring for adverse effects of OAT3 substrates is necessary, and substrate doses should be reduced according to their product labeling. 17. Ciprofloxacin and valbenazine both prolong the QTc interval. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 18. Ciprofloxacin and vandetanib both increase each other's toxicity by prolonging the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative drugs should be used. If QT-prolonging drugs must be used, frequent ECG monitoring is recommended. 19. Ciprofloxacin and vemurafenib both prolong the QTc interval. Concomitant use is not recommended, and alternative drugs should be considered. 20. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of venetoclax by inhibiting hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative drugs should be used. If a moderate CYP3A inhibitor must be used, the venetoclax dose should be reduced by at least 50%. Close monitoring for venetoclax toxicities is necessary. 21. Ciprofloxacin increases the toxicity of vilanterol/fluticasone furoate inhaled by prolonging the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative drugs should be used. Extreme caution is required when vilanterol is co-administered with drugs that prolong the QTc interval, as adrenergic agonist effects on the cardiovascular system may be potentiated. 22. Ciprofloxacin increases the effects of vildagliptin through pharmacodynamic synergism. Hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia have been reported in patients treated concomitantly with quinolones and antidiabetic agents. Careful monitoring of blood glucose is recommended. 23. Ciprofloxacin decreases the levels or effects of vitamin K1 (phytonadione) by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is minor and unknown. 24. Ciprofloxacin and voclosporin both prolong the QTc interval. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 25. Ciprofloxacin and vorinostat both prolong the QTc interval. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 26. Ciprofloxacin increases the effects of warfarin through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 27. Zinc decreases the levels or effects of ciprofloxacin by cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. Ciprofloxacin should be administered 2 hours before or 6 hours after zinc salts. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is necessary. 28. Ciprofloxacin and ziprasidone both prolong the QTc interval. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. Ciprofloxacin has minimal effects on the QT interval but should be used cautiously in combination with other QT-prolonging drugs or in patients with other risk factors. 29. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of zolpidem by inhibiting hepatic enzyme CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is required. 30. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with ciprofloxacin use. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. Appropriate fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, and antibiotic treatment for C. difficile should be initiated. 31. Ciprofloxacin is present in human milk following intravenous and oral administration. Due to the potential risk of serious adverse reactions in breastfed infants, including arthropathy observed in juvenile animal studies, breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment and for an additional two days (five half-lives) after the last dose. Alternatively, lactating women may consider pumping and discarding breast milk during treatment and for two days after the last dose. For inhalation anthrax (post-exposure), the risk-benefit assessment of continuing breastfeeding while on ciprofloxacin may be acceptable during an anthrax exposure incident. Breastfeeding women should monitor their infants for loose or bloody stools and candidiasis (thrush or diaper rash). 32. Ciprofloxacin is metabolized in the liver, primarily by CYP1A2, with a half-life of 2–5 hours in children and 3–5 hours in adults. It is excreted in urine (30–50%) and feces (15–43%). 33. Ciprofloxacin may interact with various drugs and substances, including aminophylline, amoxicillin, amphotericin, and others. Compatibility and administration guidelines should be followed to avoid adverse effects.
